repos.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
repos.paper_summary:
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a pre-trained language model that uses deep bidirectional self-attention to process text. Unlike unidirectional models, BERT conditions on both left and right context in all layers by employing a masked language model objective, where 15% of input tokens are randomly replaced with `[MASK]`, random tokens, or kept unchanged. A second pre-training task, next sentence prediction, classifies whether two sentences appear consecutively in the corpus. Fine-tuning involves adding a single output layer for specific tasks and updating all parameters.

On the GLUE benchmark, `BERT_LARGE` achieves an average score of 82.1, outperforming OpenAI GPT’s 75.1. For SQuAD v1.1 question answering, `BERT_LARGE` reaches a Test F1 of 93.2, surpassing previous top systems by 1.5 points. On SQuAD v2.0, it attains a Test F1 of 83.1, a 5.1 point improvement over prior baselines. Ablation studies show that removing the next sentence prediction task or switching to a left-to-right architecture significantly degrades performance on natural language inference and question answering tasks. The method requires substantial compute resources, with pre-training taking four days on 16 Cloud TPUs for the larger model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: BERT pre-trains deep bidirectional representations with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction, then fine-tunes them with one added output layer.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work used feature-based or unidirectional fine-tuning methods, while BERT is the first fine-tuning model that is deeply bidirectional.

digest_headlines.heading: BERT
digest_headlines.headline: BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer, with masked language model and next sentence prediction pre-training on BooksCorpus and Wikipedia.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: BERT reaches 80.5 on the GLUE leaderboard, 83.1 test F1 on SQuAD v2.0, and 93.2 test F1 on SQuAD v1.1 with TriviaQA data.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show next sentence prediction and bidirectional pre-training each improve results, and larger models improve small tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that bidirectional pre-training generalizes to a broad set of NLP tasks with one pre-trained model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists pre-training and fine-tuning hyperparameters, GLUE task descriptions, and additional ablations on training steps and masking strategies.

repos.title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
repos.paper_summary: Chatbot Arena is an open platform that ranks large language models using crowdsourced pairwise human preference votes. Users submit prompts to two anonymous models and vote for the preferred response, generating 240K votes from 90K users across 100 languages. The system estimates model scores via Bradley-Terry coefficients, using sandwich standard errors for confidence intervals. An active sampling algorithm selects model pairs to minimize variance in these estimates, reducing the sample size required to estimate win rates to a precision of 0.2 by 54% compared to random sampling (4,400 vs. 6,800 samples). Analysis of user prompts identifies 600 topic clusters, with the largest covering only 1% of data, confirming prompt diversity. Expert validation on 160 battles shows crowd-user agreement rates between 72% and 83%, comparable to expert-expert agreement of 79% to 90%. Limitations include potential user bias toward LLM enthusiasts and a focus on helpfulness over safety.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Static benchmarks miss live human preferences, so Chatbot Arena collects pairwise votes from open crowdsourced use.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks are mostly static and ground-truth based, while live human-interaction evaluation was limited to specific organizations.

digest_headlines.heading: Human Preference Data Collection
digest_headlines.headline: Users compare two anonymous model answers to any prompt and vote, yielding around 240K votes from over 90K users.

digest_headlines.heading: From Pairwise Comparisons to Rankings
digest_headlines.headline: Ranking is defined from pairwise win probabilities using Bradley-Terry coefficients, which the authors prefer to Elo for statistical estimation.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Approximate Ranking
digest_headlines.headline: Adaptive pair sampling is specified with sandwich confidence intervals, and anomalous users are flagged by a Fisher-combined p-value test.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Crowd prompts span a long tail of topics, separate model strengths, and agree with expert votes at 72% to 83%.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Adaptive sampling needs 4,400 samples against 6,800 for random to reach win-matrix precision 0.2.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors note the user base may be biased toward hobbyists and researchers, data comes from one chat interface, and safety is not assessed.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Chatbot Arena is an open pairwise-vote platform, with a dataset of 100K votes planned for release.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers a simulation comparing bootstrap and sandwich intervals, a nonparametric Bradley-Terry extension, a p-value proof, sample prompts, and the Arena Bench procedure.

repos.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
repos.paper_summary:
DSPy is a programming model that compiles declarative language model pipelines into self-improving systems by automatically optimizing prompts and demonstrations. It replaces hard-coded prompt strings with parameterized modules, such as `ChainOfThought` or `ReAct`, which are optimized by "teleprompters." These optimizers bootstrap few-shot examples or finetune smaller models to maximize a user-defined metric.

On the GSM8K math word problem dataset, compiled DSPy programs using GPT-3.5 achieved 81.6% test accuracy, outperforming standard few-shot prompting (72.4%) and expert-created demonstrations (72.4%). For llama2-13b-chat, the best configuration reached 46.9% test accuracy, surpassing the zero-shot baseline of 9.4%. On HotPotQA multi-hop question answering, a compiled multi-hop program with GPT-3.5 achieved 45.6% answer exact match, while a finetuned T5-Large model reached 39.3% on the development set. The paper notes that compiling typically takes minutes to tens of minutes. Limitations include reliance on specific metrics for optimization and the fact that results are reported on only two case studies.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Compiler
digest_headlines.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

digest_headlines.heading: Goals of Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Math Word Problems
digest_headlines.headline: Compiled DSPy programs improve GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat on math word problems from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88%.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Complex Question Answering
digest_headlines.headline: On HotPotQA, a multihop program compiled with ensembling reaches 54.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.

repos.title: OpenVoice: Versatile Instant Voice Cloning
repos.paper_summary: OpenVoice is an instant voice cloning system that copies a speaker's tone color from a short reference clip while separately controlling emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses, intonation, and language. It splits the task into a base speaker TTS model (a modified VITS that takes style and language embeddings) and a feed-forward tone color converter. The converter uses an encoder, an invertible normalizing flow conditioned on a tone color vector, and HiFi-GAN decoding. The flow is trained with a KL loss against IPA phoneme features, which removes tone color from the content representation; the reference tone color is then inserted by running the flow in reverse. The base model was trained on about 30K sentences from four speakers, and the converter on 300K samples from 20K speakers. The paper reports no quantitative comparison against baselines; evaluation is qualitative, with audio on a demo site. Speed is 12× real-time on one A10G GPU (85 ms per second of speech). Cross-lingual cloning to unseen languages works when a base speaker exists for the target language. Limitations: emotion can be slightly neutralized in some cases, and the estimated 40× real-time upper bound is not yet reached.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Instant voice cloning needs a short reference clip, but existing methods lack style control and multi-language cloning without large multi-speaker data.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice decouples a base speaker text-to-speech model for style and language from a tone color converter that adds the reference voice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice is evaluated qualitatively rather than against baselines, reaching 12 times real-time speed on one graphics processing unit.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Decoupling tone color from style and language is presented as the core principle, with code and weights released.

repos.title: When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
repos.paper_summary: This paper analyzes marginal utility in LLM test-time compute scaling, identifying that extended reasoning often degrades performance through "overthinking." The authors define a flip ratio to track when models abandon correct answers for incorrect ones as token budgets increase. Using DeepSeek-R1-32B and s1-32B on AIME 2024/2025, MATH-500, and GPQA Diamond, they measure accuracy across reasoning budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens via budget forcing. Results show marginal utility turns negative beyond 12K tokens, with the flip ratio exceeding 1.0 at approximately 7K tokens, indicating net harm from additional thinking. Easy problems (Level 1–2) exhibit overthinking at 2K tokens, while hard problems benefit up to 8K. A cost-aware evaluation framework using a tunable $\lambda$ parameter demonstrates that stopping at moderate budgets reduces computation by 50% with only 6% accuracy loss compared to peak performance. Limitations include the focus on mathematical and scientific reasoning tasks and the use of forced continuations, though natural long-reasoning samples confirm similar degradation patterns.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper tests whether more reasoning tokens keep improving accuracy and tracks answers that flip from correct to incorrect.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work reports accuracy gains with compute, and some concurrent studies document overthinking, but few measure marginal returns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Compute is measured in reasoning tokens, using budget forcing, with marginal utility, flip events, and overthinking indicators defined.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Two 32B models show accuracy peaking near 12K tokens and flip ratios above 1 from about 7K tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Cost-Aware Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Cost-weighted scoring favors stopping near 6K tokens, which yields about 50% compute reduction for about 6% accuracy loss.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Marginal utility falls at high budgets and models overthink, so the authors urge reporting efficiency frontiers alongside accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only math and science tasks and open-weight models, and causal mechanisms of overthinking remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The authors argue that identifying wasted extra computation can reduce energy use and emissions from language model inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers how natural long-reasoning samples were selected, their accuracy by output length, and their reconsideration patterns.

repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: AgentScope: A Flexible yet Robust Multi-Agent Platform
repos.paper_summary: AgentScope is a Python-based multi-agent platform that uses message exchange as its core communication mechanism. It provides pipelines and a message hub to structure agent workflows, along with pre-built agents for dialogue, code execution, and image generation. The system handles fault tolerance through service-level retries, rule-based format correction, and customizable handlers for model-resolvable errors. For distributed deployment, an actor-based framework allows developers to use identical workflow code for both local and remote execution without modifying the application logic. Multi-modal data is transmitted via URLs in messages, employing lazy loading to reduce bandwidth overhead during inter-agent communication. A drag-and-drop workstation generates JSON configurations or Python scripts from visual DAGs, enabling non-programmers to build applications. Tool usage follows a ReAct pattern where a service toolkit manages function registration, prompt engineering, and response parsing. The paper does not provide quantitative benchmarks comparing AgentScope against other frameworks like AutoGen or LangChain; instead, it documents architectural features and API interfaces. Limitations include the reliance on LLM capabilities for semantic error detection and the requirement for human intervention when unresolvable errors, such as expired API keys, occur.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent application development is hard, so the paper proposes AgentScope, a platform built around message exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Overview
digest_headlines.headline: AgentScope defines four core concepts (message, agent, service, workflow) and a three-layer architecture.

digest_headlines.heading: High Usability
digest_headlines.headline: Pipelines, a message hub, built-in agents, and a drag-and-drop workstation are offered to reduce development effort.

digest_headlines.heading: Fault-Tolerant Mechanisms
digest_headlines.headline: Errors are sorted into four levels, each handled by retries, rule-based correction, customizable handlers, or logging.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Modal Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-modal data is passed as URLs in messages, with files loaded only when needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Tool Usage
digest_headlines.headline: The service toolkit implements a ReAct loop with four steps: function preparation, instructions, reasoning, and acting.

digest_headlines.heading: Agents with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: Retrieval-augmented generation support uses a one-file configuration and shared knowledge banks that agents can update and weight.

digest_headlines.heading: Actor-based Distributed Framework
digest_headlines.headline: An actor-based distributed mode lets the same workflow run locally or across machines, using placeholder messages.

digest_headlines.heading: Signature Applications of AgentScope
digest_headlines.headline: Example applications include basic and group conversation, a six-player werewolf game, a retrieval-augmented generation copilot, web search, and a database query agent.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related frameworks such as LangChain, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev are grouped into language agent and multi-agent frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that AgentScope lowers barriers to multi-agent development and lists RAG and adaptive protocols as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix points to a GitHub repository and lists example dialogue histories for standalone conversation and werewolf.

repos.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
repos.paper_summary:
ChatDev is a multi-agent software development framework that uses LLM-driven agents to execute design, coding, and testing phases through structured dialogue. The system organizes work via a "chat chain," which breaks tasks into subtasks handled by pairs of agents acting as instructor and assistant. A "communicative dehallucination" mechanism reduces errors by having the assistant request specific details before generating code.

Evaluated on a dataset of 1,200 software requirements, ChatDev outperforms GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT. In Table 1, ChatDev achieves an executability score of 0.880 and a quality score of 0.395, compared to 0.415 and 0.152 for MetaGPT. Pairwise evaluations in Table 2 show ChatDev winning 77.1% of comparisons against GPT-Engineer when judged by GPT-4. Ablations in Table 4 indicate that removing agent roles drops executability from 0.880 to 0.580. Limitations include high computational costs due to multiple agents and a tendency to generate simple logic or static placeholders rather than complex database interactions, making it suitable primarily for prototypes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev uses chat among role-playing LLM agents, with language as the shared medium, across design, coding, and testing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers LLM agents and deep learning applied to single waterfall phases, which the authors say remain isolated.

digest_headlines.heading: ChatDev
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev pairs an instructor agent and an assistant agent per subtask, linked by a chat chain and dehallucination rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev scores highest on all four metrics and wins most pairwise comparisons against GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Authors conclude that language-based multi-agent communication improves software optimization and supports agent autonomy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Agents need detailed requirements, evaluation covers limited dimensions, and multi-agent runs need more tokens and time.

repos.title: OpenPose: Realtime Multi-Person 2D Pose Estimation using Part Affinity Fields
repos.paper_summary:
OpenPose is a bottom-up system for realtime multi-person 2D pose estimation that uses Part Affinity Fields (PAFs) to associate body parts with individuals. The method employs a multi-stage CNN, initialized from VGG-19, to predict confidence maps for part locations and PAFs, which are 2D vector fields encoding limb position and orientation. A key architectural change refines only the PAFs across stages before predicting confidence maps, rather than refining both simultaneously; this reduces computation per stage by half while increasing accuracy by approximately 7% and runtime performance by 200%.

On the MPII dataset, the method achieves 75.6% mean Average Precision using a three-scale search, outperforming DeeperCut by 13% absolute mAP on the full test set. Inference takes 0.005 s per image on a subset of 288 images, compared to 230 s for DeeperCut. The authors also release a foot keypoint dataset containing 15K instances and show that a combined body-and-foot model maintains individual component accuracy while reducing inference time relative to sequential processing. Limitations include the reliance on greedy bipartite matching for parsing, which approximates the NP-hard global optimization problem, and the top-down approach used for hand and face detection based on body keypoints.

repos.title: Fish Audio S2 Technical Report
repos.paper_summary: Fish Audio S2 is an open-source text-to-speech system that uses a Dual-Autoregressive architecture to generate multi-speaker audio with natural-language control. The model employs a Qwen3-4B backbone for semantic token prediction and a 4-layer network for acoustic detail reconstruction. Training involves a data pipeline that filters audio using a speech quality model and generates rich transcriptions via an ASR model, which are reused as reward signals during Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training. On the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark, Fish Audio S2 achieves a Word Error Rate of 0.54% in Chinese and 0.99% in English, outperforming CosyVoice 3-1.5B (1.12% and 2.21%, respectively). In production on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, the system reaches a Real-Time Factor of 0.195 and a time-to-first-audio latency of 100 ms. Evaluation on the Emergent TTS Eval shows an 81.88% win rate against a baseline. A limitation is that performance lags behind MiniMax Speech and ElevenLabs in low-resource languages with under 1,000 hours of training data.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-grained speech control lacks training data at scale, so the report pairs a data pipeline with reinforcement-learning alignment.

digest_headlines.heading: Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: The codec is streaming-capable, and generation splits a slow semantic model from a fast 4-layer acoustic model.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage pipeline separates vocals, filters with a speech quality model, and annotates speech with a rich-transcription model, whose outputs also serve as rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training runs in four stages, from a 446-million-parameter tokenizer through over 10 million hours of pre-training to reinforcement-learning post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Inference Engine
digest_headlines.headline: Streaming inference built on SGLang reaches an RTF of 0.195 and first audio in as little as 100 ms on one high-end accelerator.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Fish Audio S2 reports the lowest error rate on Chinese and English voice-cloning benchmarks and in 11 of 24 languages on the multilingual testset.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The report concludes that its architecture, dual-purpose data pipeline and multi-reward RL support controllable, multi-speaker speech, and that weights and code are released.

digest_headlines.heading: Author
digest_headlines.headline: Core contributors are ranked by contribution, and the other contributors are shuffled with a fixed seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes the Fish Audio Instruction Benchmark's construction, Gemini 3 Pro judging metrics, and its human-agreement checks.
